chapters.1: Isaiah opens by accusing Judah and Jerusalem of rebelling against God despite his care for them, comparing the nation to a body covered in untreated wounds. God says he is tired of empty religious rituals and sacrifices offered by people whose hands are stained with injustice, and calls them instead to stop doing evil, defend the oppressed, and turn back to him. He promises that if they repent their sins can be washed clean, but if they keep rebelling they will be destroyed.
chapters.2: Isaiah envisions a future day when Jerusalem will be the center of worship for all nations and war will give way to lasting peace. In the meantime, though, he condemns Judah for being full of idols, foreign customs, and pride, warning that a 'day of the Lord' is coming when human arrogance and false gods will be humbled and people will hide in terror from God's majesty.
chapters.3: Isaiah warns that God is about to strip Jerusalem and Judah of their leaders and resources, leaving the nation in chaos with inexperienced or oppressive rulers. He specifically condemns the arrogance and vanity of the wealthy women of Zion, describing how their fine jewelry and clothing will be replaced with shame, mourning, and the ravages of war.
chapters.4: This short chapter continues describing the devastation of war, picturing so many men killed that seven women compete for one husband. It then shifts to hope, promising that a faithful remnant left in Jerusalem will be called holy and cleansed, protected by God's presence like a cloud by day and fire by night.
chapters.5: Isaiah tells a parable of a vineyard owner who cared for his vineyard perfectly, yet it produced only wild, worthless grapes, representing God's disappointment with Israel's injustice despite his care for them. He pronounces a series of 'woes' against greed, drunkenness, moral confusion (calling evil good and good evil), and corruption, warning that a foreign invading army is coming as judgment.
chapters.6: Isaiah describes his dramatic vision of God on his throne surrounded by seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy,' which leaves him overwhelmed by his own sinfulness until an angel purifies his lips with a burning coal. God then commissions Isaiah as a prophet, warning him that the people will not listen and that the land will be devastated, though a small remnant will eventually remain.
chapters.7: When Judah's King Ahaz is threatened by an alliance of Syria and Israel, Isaiah urges him to trust God rather than panic, and offers him a sign. Ahaz refuses to ask for one, so God gives a sign anyway: a child will be born called Immanuel ('God with us'), and before the child is grown the threatening kingdoms will fall, though Judah itself will later face devastating conflict with Assyria.
chapters.8: Isaiah has a son given the symbolic name Maher-shalal-hash-baz, signaling that Damascus and Samaria will soon be plundered by Assyria. Because the people rejected God's quiet guidance and trusted in political alliances instead, Isaiah warns that the Assyrian flood will overwhelm the land, even reaching Judah, but he encourages the faithful to trust God rather than fear or seek answers from mediums.
chapters.9: This chapter contains the famous prophecy of a child who will be given titles like 'Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace,' bringing light to a people in darkness and establishing an everlasting, just kingdom from David's throne. The rest of the chapter pronounces judgment on Israel's northern tribes (Ephraim and Samaria) for their pride and corrupt leadership, repeating the refrain that God's anger is not yet finished with them.
chapters.10: Isaiah condemns corrupt rulers who exploit the poor, then describes Assyria as the instrument God is using to punish Israel, even though Assyria arrogantly thinks its conquests are its own achievement. God promises that once he finishes using Assyria to discipline his people, he will punish Assyria's pride in turn and preserve a faithful remnant, while describing the Assyrian army's advance toward Jerusalem in vivid, place-by-place detail before God cuts it down.
chapters.11: Isaiah prophesies a future ruler ('a rod out of the stem of Jesse') who will be filled with God's Spirit and will judge with perfect wisdom and fairness, especially for the poor. Under this ruler's reign, Isaiah pictures a world transformed into peaceful harmony (the wolf lying down with the lamb), and describes God regathering his scattered people from exile back to their land.
chapters.12: This short chapter is a psalm of thanksgiving, anticipating the day when God's people will praise him for turning away his anger and becoming their salvation. It calls on Israel to joyfully proclaim God's greatness and saving deeds to all nations.
chapters.13: This chapter is a judgment oracle against Babylon, describing God mustering an army to utterly destroy the city as punishment for its pride and cruelty. Isaiah predicts Babylon's complete and permanent desolation, becoming a ruin inhabited only by wild animals, never to be resettled.
chapters.14: Isaiah promises that God will restore Israel from exile and give them rest from their oppressors, then delivers a mocking taunt-song over the fallen king of Babylon, pictured as a glorious being ('Lucifer, son of the morning') cast down from heaven for trying to exalt himself above God. The chapter closes with brief judgment oracles against Assyria and against Philistia, both of whom are warned that their apparent security will not last.
chapters.15: This chapter is an oracle of judgment against Moab, vividly describing cities being destroyed and the Moabite people fleeing in grief, with their wealth, crops, and water sources failing all around them. Isaiah expresses genuine sorrow over Moab's devastation even though it comes as judgment.
chapters.16: The judgment on Moab continues, with Isaiah urging Moab's refugees to seek protection and describing Moab's pride and false confidence as doomed to fail. He laments the loss of Moab's vineyards and harvest celebrations, and closes by specifying that within three years Moab's glory and population will be greatly diminished.
chapters.17: This chapter pronounces judgment on Damascus (Syria) and the northern kingdom of Israel (Ephraim), which was allied with it, describing both as about to be reduced to a small, defeated remnant. It ends by picturing the surrounding hostile nations as a roaring flood that God will ultimately drive back and scatter.
chapters.18: This short chapter addresses a distant land 'beyond the rivers of Ethiopia' (likely Cush/Nubia), describing messengers being sent out and warning that this proud, powerful nation will eventually be cut down like unripe grapes. It ends with a picture of that nation eventually bringing tribute to the Lord at Mount Zion.
chapters.19: This chapter is an extended oracle against Egypt, describing internal civil conflict, failed leadership, and a collapsing economy as God's judgment on the nation and its idols. Remarkably, it ends on a hopeful note, predicting that Egypt and Assyria will one day worship the true God alongside Israel, forming a blessed partnership of former enemies.
chapters.20: God commands Isaiah to act out a sign by walking around stripped and barefoot for three years, symbolizing the humiliating captivity that awaits Egypt and Ethiopia (Cush) at the hands of Assyria. The point is to warn Judah against trusting these nations for protection, since they themselves will soon be defeated and disgraced.
chapters.21: This chapter contains three short oracles: one describing a terrifying vision of Babylon's fall to invaders (Elam and Media), one brief exchange with a watchman about Edom ('Dumah') asking how much longer the night of trouble will last, and one predicting judgment on Arabia, including the Kedar tribes, within a year.
chapters.22: Isaiah laments over Jerusalem (the 'valley of vision'), criticizing its leaders for relying on military defenses and reckless partying instead of turning to God in the face of coming disaster. He then singles out a corrupt palace official named Shebna, predicting he will be removed and replaced by Eliakim, though even Eliakim's position will not last forever.
chapters.23: This chapter is a judgment oracle against the wealthy trading city of Tyre and its ally Sidon, predicting the collapse of their commercial empire as punishment for their pride. It ends with an unusual prediction that after seventy years Tyre will become prosperous again, but that its profits will eventually be dedicated to God.
chapters.24: Isaiah broadens his focus from individual nations to describe a sweeping, worldwide judgment in which the whole earth is devastated because its people have broken God's laws. Amid the desolation he includes scattered notes of praise for God's righteousness, and the chapter ends looking forward to the day when the Lord will reign gloriously from Jerusalem.
chapters.25: This is a song of praise to God for bringing down the proud and arrogant and for being a refuge for the poor and needy. It includes a famous promise that God will one day host a great feast for all peoples and permanently 'swallow up death,' wiping away tears and removing disgrace.
chapters.26: This chapter is a song of trust sung by the righteous, celebrating God as a strong fortress and source of perfect peace for those who rely on him. It contrasts the fate of the proud, who will not survive, with hope for resurrection and renewal for God's own people, who are told to wait patiently through present trouble.
chapters.27: Isaiah describes God defeating 'Leviathan,' a symbolic monster representing chaos and hostile nations, and compares Israel to a vineyard that God tends and protects. The chapter ends with a hopeful picture of scattered Israelites being gathered back from Assyria and Egypt to worship God in Jerusalem.
chapters.28: Isaiah condemns the leaders of Ephraim (the northern kingdom) for their drunkenness and poor judgment, and criticizes Judah's leaders in Jerusalem for making a false 'covenant with death' through dishonest alliances. He promises that God is laying a trustworthy 'cornerstone' for those who believe, while warning that those trusting in lies will be swept away, illustrated by a farming analogy about using the right method for each crop.
chapters.29: Isaiah warns Jerusalem (called 'Ariel') that it will face siege and distress, but promises that the attacking nations will ultimately vanish like a bad dream. He criticizes the people's empty, insincere worship and spiritual blindness, but promises a future reversal where the deaf will hear, the blind will see, and the humble will rejoice in God.
chapters.30: Isaiah condemns Judah's leaders for seeking a political alliance with Egypt instead of trusting God, warning that Egypt's help will prove worthless and bring only shame. He contrasts the people's stubborn refusal to listen with God's patient willingness to show mercy if they return to him, and closes describing devastating judgment on Assyria by God's own power.
chapters.31: Isaiah again warns against trusting Egypt's military strength instead of God, pointing out that Egypt's horses and chariots are merely human and will fail. He promises that God himself will defend Jerusalem like a protective bird and will cause Assyria to fall, prompting the people to finally abandon their idols.
chapters.32: Isaiah envisions a future king who will reign with justice, under whom corrupt and deceitful people will be exposed and honest, generous people will be honored. He warns complacent, comfortable women that hard times are coming, but promises that afterward God's Spirit will transform the land into a place of lasting peace, justice, and security.
chapters.33: Isaiah pronounces judgment on an unnamed destroyer (likely Assyria) who has plundered others and will himself be plundered, while the people cry out to God for help amid desolation. The chapter shifts to a vision of a secure, restored Zion where the righteous dwell safely, God himself serves as king and protector, and sickness and guilt are finally removed.
chapters.34: This chapter announces a sweeping judgment on all hostile nations, focusing especially on Edom, which will be devastated with bloodshed and left permanently desolate, overrun by wild animals and birds. It's presented as part of God settling his case on behalf of Zion.
chapters.35: In contrast to the devastation of surrounding nations, this chapter is a joyful vision of restoration, where deserts bloom, the blind see, the deaf hear, and the lame leap. It promises a 'highway of holiness' along which God's redeemed, ransomed people will return safely to Zion with everlasting joy.
chapters.36: This narrative chapter describes the Assyrian king Sennacherib's army besieging Jerusalem under King Hezekiah, with the Assyrian official Rabshakeh mocking Judah's trust in both Egypt and God and urging the people to surrender. Hezekiah's officials report the threatening speech back to the king without responding to Rabshakeh directly.
chapters.37: Hezekiah turns to prayer and to the prophet Isaiah after Assyria's threats, and Isaiah assures him that God will defend Jerusalem and turn back the Assyrian king. True to the promise, an angel of the Lord strikes down the Assyrian army overnight, Sennacherib retreats to Nineveh, and is later assassinated by his own sons.
chapters.38: King Hezekiah becomes critically ill, and after Isaiah tells him he will die, Hezekiah prays earnestly and God grants him fifteen more years of life, confirmed by a miraculous sign of the sun's shadow moving backward. The chapter includes Hezekiah's personal poem of gratitude for being spared from death.
chapters.39: Babylonian envoys visit the recovering Hezekiah, and he proudly shows them all his treasures and wealth. Isaiah then warns Hezekiah that because of this, Babylon will one day carry off all these treasures and even Hezekiah's own descendants into captivity, a warning Hezekiah accepts with relief that at least it won't happen in his own lifetime.
chapters.40: This chapter opens a new section of Isaiah with words of comfort for God's people, announcing that their punishment is over and that a voice is calling to prepare the way for God's coming, famously quoted about John the Baptist. It emphasizes God's unmatched power and greatness compared to the fleeting nature of humanity and the emptiness of idols, promising that those who trust in him will find renewed strength, 'mounting up with wings as eagles.'
chapters.41: God challenges the nations and their idols to a kind of courtroom debate, pointing out that he alone has raised up a conquering ruler from the east (likely Cyrus) and controls the course of history. He reassures Israel, his chosen servant, not to fear since he will strengthen and help them, while mocking the uselessness of man-made idols that people nervously nail down so they won't fall over.
chapters.42: This chapter introduces God's 'servant,' a gentle yet unstoppable figure who will bring justice to the nations without force or self-promotion, later understood as pointing to the coming Messiah. It calls for a 'new song' of praise to God for his coming victory, and contrasts this with Israel's own current blindness and deafness to God despite being his chosen servant, explaining their suffering as consequence of disobedience.
chapters.43: God reassures Israel that he will be with them through hardship ('through the waters... through the fire') and will gather his scattered people back from every direction. He declares himself the only true God and Savior, reminds Israel that he alone predicted and controls events (including judgment on Babylon), and states that he forgives their sins for his own sake even though they have grown weary of worshiping him.
chapters.44: God promises to pour out blessing and his Spirit on Israel and declares again that he is the only true God, mocking in detail the absurdity of idol-makers who craft gods out of the same wood they use for firewood. He assures Israel that their sins are forgiven and, notably, names Cyrus by name as the king God will use to rebuild Jerusalem and its temple.
chapters.45: God specifically calls out Cyrus, the Persian king, as his chosen instrument to conquer nations and free Israel from exile, even though Cyrus does not personally know God. The chapter emphasizes God's total sovereignty as Creator over all events (both good and difficult), rebukes any objection to his plans, and declares that every nation will eventually acknowledge him as the only true God.
chapters.46: Isaiah contrasts the Babylonian gods Bel and Nebo, which must be carried as a dead burden on animals, with the true God who personally carries and sustains his people from birth to old age. God reaffirms that he alone can declare the future and will certainly carry out his plans, including bringing deliverance to Zion.
chapters.47: This chapter is a judgment oracle predicting Babylon's humiliating fall from pride and luxury into shame and slavery, as punishment for its cruelty toward Israel and its arrogant self-sufficiency. Isaiah mocks Babylon's trust in astrologers and magicians, saying none of their divination will be able to save them from the coming disaster.
chapters.48: God rebukes Israel for worshiping him insincerely while still being stubborn and prone to idolatry, explaining that he announced events in advance specifically so they couldn't credit idols for what he did. He reminds them he has refined them through hardship for his own name's sake, and closes with a call to leave Babylon and declare that God has redeemed his people, punctuated by the sobering reminder that there is no peace for the wicked.
chapters.49: God's servant describes being called before birth for a mission that at first feels like a failure, but is reassured that his role will extend beyond restoring Israel to becoming 'a light to the Gentiles' reaching the ends of the earth. God promises Zion that even though she feels forgotten, he could no more forget her than a mother could forget her child, and foretells a future return of exiled children and reversal of her humiliation before the nations.
chapters.50: God insists that Israel's exile is the result of their own sin, not any failure or weakness on his part to save them. The servant figure speaks of faithfully enduring suffering, mockery, and physical abuse while trusting that God will ultimately vindicate him, and the chapter ends urging those who fear the Lord to trust him rather than rely on their own schemes.
chapters.51: God encourages Israel by pointing back to Abraham and Sarah as proof of his faithfulness, and promises to turn Zion's ruins into a flourishing, Eden-like place. He urges the people not to fear human oppressors since they are temporary, and declares that Jerusalem, which has 'drunk the cup' of his judgment, will soon have that cup of suffering taken away and handed instead to her tormentors.
chapters.52: This chapter calls Jerusalem to wake up, shake off the humiliation of captivity, and prepare for freedom and restoration, famously praising those who bring 'good tidings' of peace and salvation. It closes by introducing a mysterious, exalted 'servant' who will be badly disfigured and marred, yet will ultimately astonish many nations, setting up the description that continues in chapter 53.
chapters.53: This is the famous 'Suffering Servant' chapter, describing a figure despised, rejected, and crushed, who bears the sins and punishment of others so that they can be healed, 'wounded for our transgressions.' Though he is innocent and silent before his accusers like a lamb led to slaughter, God ultimately vindicates him, and through his suffering many are made right with God; Christians traditionally read this as a prophecy of Jesus's death.
chapters.54: Using the image of a barren woman suddenly given many children, this chapter promises that Israel, though currently diminished and in exile, will be restored with far greater numbers and security than before. God compares his relationship with Israel to a marriage, promising that though he disciplined them briefly, his compassion and covenant of peace are everlasting and no weapon formed against them will succeed.
chapters.55: God issues an open invitation for anyone thirsty or hungry to come freely receive spiritual nourishment, and urges people to seek him while he can be found and turn from wicked ways to receive mercy. The chapter includes the well-known comparison of God's word to rain that always accomplishes its purpose, closing with a joyful picture of creation celebrating Israel's restoration.
chapters.56: God promises that foreigners and eunuchs who faithfully follow him will be fully welcomed and blessed in his house, declaring that his temple will be 'a house of prayer for all people,' not just Israelites. The chapter then sharply criticizes Israel's current leaders ('watchmen'), calling them blind, lazy, and self-serving, more interested in their own gain and pleasure than guarding the people.
chapters.57: Isaiah laments that the righteous die without anyone noticing or caring, while condemning Israel for persistent idolatry, including disturbing pagan practices, comparing the nation to an unfaithful spouse. Yet God also promises comfort and healing to the humble and repentant, while reaffirming that there's 'no peace for the wicked,' who remain restless like a stormy sea.
chapters.58: God criticizes the people for going through the motions of religious fasting while still mistreating others and ignoring justice, making clear that the fasting he truly wants looks like freeing the oppressed, feeding the hungry, and caring for the needy. He promises that if the people genuinely live this way and honor the Sabbath, they'll experience healing, guidance, and lasting blessing.
chapters.59: Isaiah explains that it's the people's own sins, not any weakness in God, that have created separation from him, detailing specific sins like violence, lying, and injustice that have corrupted society. God is described as finally stepping in himself, since no human intercessor could be found, putting on 'righteousness as a breastplate' to bring judgment and ultimately redemption to those in Jacob who turn from sin.
chapters.60: Isaiah pictures Jerusalem's future glory, when its light will draw nations and kings from everywhere, bringing wealth, gifts, and even former oppressors coming humbly to serve rather than attack. The chapter promises a permanent transformation in which violence disappears, God himself becomes Jerusalem's everlasting light, and the once-small, afflicted nation becomes strong and numerous.
chapters.61: The speaker (traditionally understood as the Messiah, and quoted by Jesus in Luke 4) announces being anointed by God's Spirit to bring good news to the poor, comfort to the brokenhearted, and freedom to captives, turning mourning into joy. The chapter promises that God's people will rebuild what was ruined and be recognized among the nations as blessed, clothed in salvation and righteousness like a bride and groom.
chapters.62: Isaiah promises that Jerusalem will no longer be called 'Forsaken' or 'Desolate' but will be renamed to reflect God's delight in her, compared to a bride cherished by her husband. He calls for watchmen to keep praying without rest until the city's full restoration and renewed prosperity are complete.
chapters.63: This chapter opens with a vivid image of God returning from battle against Edom, his garments stained red from treading his enemies like grapes in a winepress, executing judgment alone. It then shifts into a prayer recalling God's past kindness and deliverance of Israel from Egypt, lamenting their rebellion and pleading with God to return and act on their behalf again.
chapters.64: This chapter continues the prayer of chapter 63, pleading for God to dramatically intervene the way he has in the past, while honestly confessing the people's sinfulness ('all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags'). It closes with a sorrowful description of Jerusalem and the temple lying in ruins, asking God not to stay angry or silent forever.
chapters.65: God answers by explaining that he has been reaching out to a stubborn, idolatrous people who ignored him, and promises a clear separation: faithful 'servants' will be blessed with joy and abundance while the rebellious will face shame and judgment. The chapter ends with the famous promise of 'new heavens and a new earth,' a transformed Jerusalem full of joy, long life, and peace, even among once-hostile animals.
chapters.66: Isaiah stresses that God values humility and genuine obedience far more than empty rituals or sacrifices performed insincerely. The book closes with a vision of Jerusalem's sudden, joyful restoration compared to an instant birth, a promise that people from all nations will come to worship God, and a stark final contrast between those who will be comforted and blessed and the rebellious who will face lasting judgment.
